outcome: No public work since 26 January 2024 that I could find settles or moves Szymanski's conjecture as stated: the one in-window paper on the topic (Chakrabarty and Seshadhri, arXiv September 2024, ITCS 2025) concerns a layered directed hypercube and does not mention the doubly directed cube or permutation routing, so the problem is still listed as open, with the n ≤ 4 computer verification (1999/2001) the last positive case I could attribute.
problem_asks: (1) For every dimension n ≥ 1: the conjecture is universal over n. (2) For every permutation π of the 2ⁿ vertices of the doubly directed n-cube Qₙ (all permutations, not some). (3) One system of directed paths, one path for each vertex v, running from v to π(v); a path may be trivial when π(v) = v. (4) Arc-disjointness: no two of these paths use the same edge in the same direction; the two directions of one edge are separate resources. (5) No bound on path length: the statement says 'paths', not 'shortest paths'. (6) One simultaneous routing, not a routing split into rounds or parts. A yes-answer for all n settles every part. A counterexample is one pair (n, π) for which no such system exists. Not asked by the statement, but often confused with it: (a) the stronger shortest-path variant (Szymanski's own additional proposal, per Wikipedia and search snippets); (b) 2-rearrangeability, where π is split into two pieces each routable (weaker); (c) 2-1 routing requests, where a vertex may be a source twice but a target only once (different question).

events.what_happened: Baudon, Fertin and Havel report, by computer search, that for every permutation of the 16 vertices of the directed 4-cube H4 there is a system of pairwise arc-disjoint directed paths from each vertex to its image. Wikipedia cites this paper for the statement that computer experiments verified the conjecture for n ≤ 4. First public written form: the conference paper 'Routing permutations in the hypercube' (WG'99, Ascona; Springer LNCS, pp. 179–190). Journal version: 'Routing permutations and 2-1 routing requests in the hypercube', Discrete Applied Mathematics 113(1) (2001) 43–58. The journal version also shows that for n ≥ 3 some 2-1 routing request cannot be routed by arc-disjoint paths; that is a different question and is not counted here.
events.revisions: Journal version DAM 113(1), 2001, pp. 43–58, extends the conference paper. Both versions are deposited on HAL with a December 2011 date (repository date, not first public).
events.delivers: For n = 4 only: every permutation of the vertices of the doubly directed 4-cube is routed by pairwise arc-disjoint directed paths. This is a finite check of one dimension, and it is a case of the statement's universal claim. Wikipedia's n ≤ 4 wording also covers n ≤ 3, but no source for n ≤ 3 is attributed to this event.
events.remains: Every n ≥ 5 (all permutations of Qₙ, arbitrary-length paths). The smaller cases n ≤ 3 are not established by this event alone.

events.what_happened: Anna Lubiw, 'Counterexample to a conjecture of Szymanski on hypercube routing', Information Processing Letters 35(2) (1990) 57–61 (DOI 10.1016/0020-0190(90)90106-8). Per Wikipedia and search snippets, it shows that Szymanski's stronger proposal, that every permutation can be routed with shortest paths, fails: some permutations need paths that are not shortest. Wikipedia attributes the n ≥ 5 non-shortest-path permutations to this paper. One search snippet describes a 5-dimensional example; I could not read the paper to confirm the dimension.
events.delivers: Shows that the shortest-path version fails: some permutations of the cube cannot be routed by edge-disjoint shortest paths (for n ≥ 5 per Wikipedia). The statement as written allows paths of any length, so this does not refute it.
events.remains: The statement as written, for every n and every permutation, with arbitrary-length arc-disjoint paths. The counterexample leaves it untouched.

events.what_happened: Qian-Ping Gu and Hisao Tamaki, 'Routing a permutation in the hypercube by two sets of edge disjoint paths', Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 44(2) (1997) 147–152. Per Wikipedia: every permutation of the hypercube can be split into two partial permutations, each routable by edge-disjoint paths (2-rearrangeability). One search snippet attributed this result to Goldberg and Tarjan (1997) instead. The paper itself was not read. See disputes.
events.delivers: Every permutation of the cube splits into two partial permutations, each routed by edge-disjoint paths. This is a weaker property than one system routing the whole permutation, so it settles no case of the statement.
events.remains: The one-system claim for every n and every permutation.

events.what_happened: Xiaojun Shen, Qing Hu and Weifa Liang, 'Realization of an arbitrary permutation on a hypercube', Information Processing Letters 51(5) (1994) 237–243 (received 15 October 1993, revised 28 April 1994). Per the CityU record and a search snippet: an explicit combinatorial algorithm builds a 2-realization of any permutation on a d-cube, with total directed-edge usage (counting repetitions) within d·2ᵈ. A corollary gives a (2d−3)-step realization on a packet-switched d-cube for d ≥ 3. The PDF was not readable, so this description comes from the listing abstract.
events.delivers: A constructive 2-realization of every permutation. That is a weaker property than one edge-disjoint system for the whole permutation. Its packet-switched corollary is a different model. It settles no case of the statement.
events.remains: The one-system claim for every n and every permutation.

events.what_happened: Jop Briët, Sourav Chakraborty, David García-Soriano and Arie Matsliah, 'Monotonicity testing and shortest-path routing on the cube'. First public written form: ECCC report TR10-048, dated 24 March 2010. Conference version: RANDOM 2010 (LNCS 6302, pp. 462–475). Journal version: Combinatorica 32(1) (2012) 35–53 (DOI 10.1007/s00493-012-2765-1). Per abstract text quoted in search results (the paper PDF was not readable): they build instances with Ω(2ⁿ) source–sink pairs in which at most roughly a 1/√n fraction of pairs can be connected simultaneously by edge-disjoint paths, answering a question of Lehman and Ron. They also show that for any δ > 0 the n-cube is not n^(1/2−δ)-realizable with shortest paths, where previously only non-1-realizability was known. The ECCC abstract page describes the construction, in its own words, as 'a strong counterexample to Szymanski's conjecture on routing in the hypercube'.
events.revisions: ECCC TR10-048 (March 2010); RANDOM 2010 conference version; Combinatorica 32(1), 2012. The first public written form is the ECCC report.
events.delivers: Shortest-path variant: fails with a quantitative bound (no n^(1/2−δ)-realizability by shortest paths). Edge-disjoint variant: a fraction bound on pairs connectable by edge-disjoint paths, for an instance family on the cube. Whether that family consists of permutations of the doubly directed n-cube, with arbitrary-length paths, is not established by anything I could read. The sources point the other way: the edge-disjoint setting appears to be the layered directed hypercube of Lehman and Ron, not the doubly directed cube (see doubts).
events.remains: Whatever part of the statement the edge-disjoint bound does not reach. If it concerns the doubly directed cube and full permutations, it bears on the statement. If not, the statement is untouched. The shortest-path result is clearly a different question.

(2) Evidence the other way: the Lehman–Ron setting is the layered directed cube, and the edge-disjoint negative result for paths following a matching (cited as BCSM12 in the Chakrabarty–Seshadhri summary) is in that setting. Also a construction showing that for every δ > 0 the n-cube is not n^(1/2−δ)-realizable with shortest paths. Whether either is explicit or non-constructive is not established; I could not read the construction.

events.what_happened: Deeparnab Chakrabarty and C. Seshadhri, 'Directed Hypercube Routing, a Generalized Lehman-Ron Theorem, and Monotonicity Testing', arXiv:2409.02206 (v1 submitted 3 September 2024), published at ITCS 2025 (LIPIcs vol. 325, pp. 34:1–34:15). They prove that for a matched pair of sets S ⊆ Lᵢ and T ⊆ Lⱼ in the directed hypercube, with j − i ≥ 2, there are two edge-disjoint collections of vertex-disjoint paths between S and T, strengthening the Lehman–Ron theorem (which gives one collection). They also state conjectures on directed-hypercube flows and derive isoperimetric consequences for monotonicity testing. The paper does not mention Szymanski or permutation routing, per my reading of the abstract and HTML text.
events.revisions: v2 submitted 4 December 2024 (typos fixed, related-paper references updated). Published at ITCS 2025; the Dagstuhl record gives 11 February 2025.
events.delivers: In the layered directed hypercube: for a matched pair of sets in layers at least two apart, two edge-disjoint families of vertex-disjoint paths. The terminals are a matched pair S → T, not a permutation of all vertices; the paths need not follow the matching; the graph is the directed layered cube as I read the setting (arc orientation was not confirmed from text). It gives no path system in the doubly directed cube and no routing of any permutation there.
events.remains: All of the statement: the doubly directed cube, every permutation, one prescribed target per vertex. The flow conjectures in the paper are open.

events.what_happened: William Duckworth and Alan Gibbons, 'Hypercubic combinatorics: Hamiltonian decomposition and permutation routing', Journal of Combinatorial Mathematics and Combinatorial Computing 63 (2007) 145–158. Shows that any permutation of the d-cube can be routed in at most 2d−1 steps without queueing, with off-line path systems. This is a time-stepped queueless model, not one simultaneous arc-disjoint routing. The year is from the ANU repository record and a search summary.

disputes.summary: Who proved that the hypercube is 2-rearrangeable (any permutation splits into two partial permutations, each routable by edge-disjoint paths). The Wikipedia reference list, as fetched through a summarising fetch, gives Gu and Tamaki (1997). One search snippet attributed the result to Goldberg and Tarjan (1997). The Gu–Tamaki title matches the Wikipedia citation. Not resolved: I did not read the 1997 paper or the Wikipedia wikitext verbatim.

The authors of the 2010/2012 Briët et al. paper describe their construction as a strong counterexample to Szymanski's conjecture on routing in the hypercube (ECCC abstract page). The Wikipedia article, as fetched, still lists the conjecture as open and presents the shortest-path result as a separate matter. The difference rests on whether the edge-disjoint bound applies to the doubly directed cube with arbitrary paths, which I could not establish from the readable text.

summary: Szymanski's conjecture asks whether every permutation of the doubly directed n-cube can be routed by arc-disjoint paths of any length, for every n. As of the Wikipedia article I could reach (through a summarising fetch, not verbatim), it is still listed as open. The positive knowledge is finite and older: Baudon, Fertin and Havel verified the n = 4 case by computer (WG'99, DAM 2001); Wikipedia's n ≤ 4 wording also covers smaller n, but no source for n ≤ 3 is attributed to this event. Gu and Tamaki (1997, per Wikipedia) proved 2-rearrangeability, a weaker property. Lubiw (1990) showed that the stronger shortest-path variant fails, which does not refute the statement because the statement allows longer paths. Briët, Chakraborty, García-Soriano and Matsliah (ECCC, March 2010; Combinatorica 2012) give a quantitative shortest-path counterexample and an edge-disjoint fraction bound, and the ECCC page calls the construction 'a strong counterexample to Szymanski's conjecture'. Whether the edge-disjoint bound concerns the doubly directed cube with full permutations and arbitrary paths is the central close call. Reading for: the bound is in the layered directed hypercube of Lehman and Ron. Support: the follow-up result on edge-disjoint paths following a matching (cited as BCSM12 in the Chakrabarty–Seshadhri summary) is in that layered setting, and the Lehman–Ron literature treats the directed cube, not the doubly directed one. Reading against: the authors describe the result as a counterexample to Szymanski's conjecture, and the paper's own definitions were unreadable to me, so I could not confirm the setting. In the window since 26 January 2024, the only paper on the topic that I found is Chakrabarty and Seshadhri (arXiv 3 September 2024; ITCS 2025). It generalises Lehman–Ron for the layered directed cube with two edge-disjoint vertex-disjoint path collections. It does not mention Szymanski or permutation routing, and it does not address the statement. On AI involvement: I searched explicitly for AI with this problem's name across lab announcements, AI-counterexample surveys, AlphaEvolve, OpenAI, Gemini Deep Think, Claude and Grok, Erdős-problem trackers, and the formal-conjectures benchmark. No source names an AI system as contributing to this problem. Nearby AI work on other problems is listed as dead ends. The Manifold market (81% YES on 'a widely accepted proof') is a secondary sentiment signal and is not evidence about the mathematics.
competing_reading: The Briët et al. edge-disjoint bound, with its authors' own description as a 'strong counterexample to Szymanski's conjecture', is a refutation of the statement, not merely of the shortest-path variant. On that reading the problem is no longer open, and the 1999/2001 n = 4 check and the 2010 result together settle its status against the conjecture. Against that reading: Wikipedia as fetched still lists the conjecture as open; the authors' edge-disjoint setting is most likely the layered directed hypercube, which is not the statement's doubly directed cube; and their shortest-path counterexample does not reach the statement. Separately, a reader could say the n = 4 computer check is a finite instance of a universal claim and so 'moves nothing'. Another could say it is a restricted case the problem asks for, since Wikipedia counts it.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Briët et al. (CWI PDF or Combinatorica 2012): the definition of the cube used in the edge-disjoint lower bound (doubly directed or layered directed), whether the instances are full permutations, and whether the paths are required to be shortest. (2) The verbatim current Wikipedia article, to see how it treats the Briët et al. result and the n ≤ 4 claim. (3) The Baudon, Fertin and Havel DAM 2001 text, to confirm the scope of the n = 4 computation and any n ≤ 3 claim. (4) The Lubiw 1990 paper, to confirm the dimension of her counterexample and its exact scope. (5) The Gu–Tamaki 1997 abstract, to settle the attribution dispute. (6) Any later paper that cites Briët et al. or Baudon et al. and states the status of the statement.

judgement.why: The only post-snapshot event, Chakrabarty–Seshadhri (arXiv September 2024), generalises Lehman–Ron for vertex-disjoint paths between matched layer sets in the layered directed cube. It does not route permutations of the doubly directed cube, so it is a variant. All other events predate 2024. Baudon–Fertin–Havel settles the whole of dimension n = 4 for every permutation, so it is a restriction of a statement that is universal over n. I scored it case, not instances, because it settles one complete dimension rather than sampling permutations. It was published in DAM, so it counts as digested. Lubiw and the shortest-path half of Briët et al. answer Szymanski's stronger shortest-path proposal. 2-rearrangeability, 2-realization, step-count routing models and 2-1 requests are different questions. All of those are variants. The close call is Briët et al.'s edge-disjoint fraction bound, which the ECCC page calls a 'strong counterexample to Szymanski's conjecture'. The record's evidence places that bound in the layered (Lehman–Ron) directed cube with source–sink pairs, not full permutations of the doubly directed cube with arbitrary paths. Wikipedia still lists the conjecture as open. So I scored it variant rather than a refutation. No AI involvement in any event.
judgement.doubts: The Briët et al. scope rests on abstracts. If its edge-disjoint instances turn out to be permutations of the doubly directed cube, it would be a pre-snapshot refutation (resolved, so open_stale), not a variant. That would not change the post-snapshot picture. The n = 4 scope and the Lubiw dimension are from listings and snippets only.
